concepts.name: Origins and Evolution of Judicial Activism in India
key_dimensions: Shift from judicial restraint to activism post-Emergency (1970s–80s)
Role of Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer as pioneers
Contrast with US judicial activism and doctrine of originalism
Triggering factors: executive overreach, legislative vacuum, rights violations

concepts.name: Locus Standi Relaxation and the Birth of PIL
key_dimensions: Traditional rule: only aggrieved party can approach court (locus standi)
Hussainara Khatoon (1979) as the first landmark PIL case on undertrial prisoners
Epistolary jurisdiction: letters/postcards treated as writ petitions
Distinction between PIL in India vs. class action suits in the USA

concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of PIL and Judicial Activism
key_dimensions: Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) as the foundation for PIL
Article 21 (Right to Life) expansively interpreted to justify activism
Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid) as a DPSP backing PIL
Absence of explicit PIL provision — entirely judge-made law

concepts.name: Types and Classification of PILs
key_dimensions: Social action PILs vs. adversarial PILs (private interest disguised as public)
Environmental PILs, prison reform PILs, electoral reform PILs
suo motu cognizance by courts as a variant of PIL jurisdiction
PILs against government inaction vs. PILs challenging legislation

concepts.name: Landmark PIL Cases and Their Constitutional Significance
key_dimensions: S.P. Gupta vs. Union of India (1981): open standing, judges' transfer
M.C. Mehta cases: Oleum gas leak, Ganga pollution, absolute liability doctrine
Vishaka vs. State of Rajasthan (1997): guidelines as law in absence of legislation
Vineet Narain case (1997): CBI independence and 'Hawala' scandal

concepts.name: Absolute Liability Doctrine vs. Strict Liability (Rylands v. Fletcher)
key_dimensions: Strict liability origin: Rylands v. Fletcher (UK, 1868) — allows exceptions
Absolute liability introduced in M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India (Oleum gas, 1986)
No exceptions under absolute liability for hazardous enterprises
UPSC trap: Absolute liability is Indian judicial innovation, stricter than strict liability

concepts.name: Judicial Legislation and the Separation of Powers Debate
key_dimensions: Vishaka guidelines as quasi-legislation until POSH Act 2013
NALSA judgment (2014) on transgender rights creating new legal category
Criticism: Courts encroaching on Parliament's domain (counter-majoritarian difficulty)
Doctrine of 'constitutional silence' used to justify judicial lawmaking

concepts.name: Suo Motu Jurisdiction as an Instrument of Judicial Activism
key_dimensions: Definition: Court takes cognizance on its own without a petition
Constitutional basis: inherent powers under Articles 32, 136, 226, 142
Recent examples: COVID-19 management, oxygen supply, migrant workers
Controversy: democratic legitimacy of unilateral court intervention

concepts.name: Article 142 and the 'Complete Justice' Doctrine
key_dimensions: Text of Article 142: SC may pass any order to do 'complete justice'
Used in Bhopal Gas case settlement, Ayodhya verdict land allocation
Criticism: 'nuclear missile against gnats' — disproportionate use
UPSC trap: Article 142 is available ONLY to Supreme Court, not High Courts

concepts.name: Court-Appointed Committees and Continuing Mandamus
key_dimensions: Continuing mandamus: ongoing judicial supervision of government compliance
Court-appointed committees (e.g., Lodha Committee for BCCI reforms)
Central Empowered Committee for forest matters under Supreme Court
Tension between judicial monitoring and executive autonomy

concepts.name: PIL and Environmental Jurisprudence
key_dimensions: Precautionary principle, polluter pays principle — judicially incorporated
M.C. Mehta series: Taj Trapezium, Vehicular pollution in Delhi, Ganga cleaning
National Green Tribunal Act 2010: partly a response to PIL overload in courts
Distinction: NGT jurisdiction vs. Supreme Court PIL on environment

concepts.name: Judicial Overreach: Criticism and Limits of Judicial Activism
key_dimensions: BCCI case: SC restructuring a private body — boundary of public law
Delhi liquor policy, coal block allocation — courts reviewing policy decisions
Doctrine of proportionality as a check on judicial overreach
Former CJI critiques: 'PIL has become Publicity Interest Litigation'

concepts.name: Guidelines for Admission and Rejection of PILs
key_dimensions: SC guidelines (2010) to curb frivolous PILs: bench scrutiny at admission stage
Imposition of costs on frivolous PILs as deterrent
PIL not maintainable in service matters, contractual disputes (settled law)
UPSC trap: PILs can be filed only in SC (Art. 32) and HC (Art. 226), not subordinate courts

concepts.name: Judicial Activism vs. Judicial Restraint: Doctrinal Comparison
key_dimensions: Judicial restraint: court defers to legislature/executive on policy (e.g., early SC era)
Political question doctrine as a tool of restraint (non-justiciable matters)
Activism justified by 'constitutional morality' concept (Navtej Johar, 2018)
Balance test: activism appropriate when other institutions fail, not as routine

concepts.name: PIL and Fundamental Rights Expansion (Article 21 Jurisprudence)
key_dimensions: Maneka Gandhi (1978): broadened Article 21 to include procedure that is fair, just, reasonable
PIL used to enforce positive obligations of state under Article 21
Right to health, education, livelihood, environment derived via PIL route
UPSC trap: Article 21 rights are available to non-citizens too, not just citizens

concepts.name: Contempt of Court Powers and Judicial Accountability in Activism
key_dimensions: Contempt of Courts Act 1971: civil contempt vs. criminal contempt
Used to enforce PIL-based orders (e.g., pollution control compliance)
Criticism: contempt powers insulate judiciary from accountability
Article 129 (SC) and Article 215 (HC): constitutional basis of contempt jurisdiction

concepts.name: Epistolary Jurisdiction and Access to Justice
key_dimensions: Letters to judges treated as writ petitions — unique Indian innovation
Sunil Batra case (1978): letter from prisoner led to prison reforms
Democratization of justice: removes barrier of legal representation for poor
Current status: epistolary jurisdiction used sparingly by modern SC

concepts.name: PIL in Electoral Reforms and Democratic Accountability
key_dimensions: Association for Democratic Reforms (2002): mandatory disclosure of criminal antecedents by candidates
PUCL vs. Union of India (2013): NOTA introduced via judicial direction
Court directions on electoral bond transparency (2024 SBI case)
Boundary issue: judiciary directing Election Commission — constitutional tension

concepts.name: Comparative PIL: India vs. Other Jurisdictions
key_dimensions: USA: Class action suits under Federal Rules — party-driven, not judge-driven
Pakistan and Bangladesh adopted PIL concept from India
UK: no equivalent — parliamentary sovereignty limits judicial activism
India's PIL unique: combination of relaxed standing + epistolary + suo motu

concepts.name: Judicial Activism and the Basic Structure Doctrine Interface
key_dimensions: Kesavananda Bharati (1973): judicial activism at its peak — limiting Parliament
Basic structure as a judicially created doctrine with no textual basis
Minerva Mills (1980): balance between FRs and DPSPs restored by activism
UPSC trap: Basic structure doctrine applies only to constitutional amendments, not ordinary legislation
